Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following pair of headlines and opening lines from two newspapers reporting the same student protest.

Newspaper A: 'Thousands of students march for affordable housing' – Students filled the city centre on Saturday, chanting and carrying handmade banners, to demand rent controls.
Newspaper B: 'Student mob brings city centre to standstill' – Shoppers were left stranded on Saturday as crowds of students blocked roads, causing chaos for local businesses.

Guiding question: How do the two newspapers shape readers' opinions of the same event?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the same facts are framed as civic action (A) and disruption (B). (1) Diction: "march" versus "mob". (2) Whose perspective is centred. (3) A includes the demand; B omits it. Evaluation: neither is strictly false; framing operates through selection and connotation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Thesis: the same facts are framed as civic action (A) and disruption (B). (1) Diction: "march" versus "mob". (2) Whose perspective is centred. (3) A includes the demand; B omits it. Evaluation: neither is strictly false; framing operates through selection and connotation. Paper 1 criteria (5 marks each, 20 total). A Understanding and interpretation: grasp of the literal and implied meaning, references well chosen. B Analysis and evaluation: how textual features and authorial choices shape meaning, with evaluation of their effect. C Focus and organisation: a clear line of argument that answers the guiding question (or a chosen focus) and is developed coherently. D Language: clear, precise, varied academic register and accurate terminology. 5 = excellent, 3 = adequate, 1 = minimal.

Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following direct-mail appeal letter from an international charity.

Dear Friend,
This is Amina. She is seven. Every morning she walks two hours to collect water that makes her sick.
[Photograph: a thin girl with downcast eyes holds a yellow jerrycan.]
For just 5 euros a month, you can change Amina's life forever.
Please don't turn the page.

Guiding question: How does the appeal attempt to persuade its readers, and what ethical questions does it raise?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the appeal is persuasive because it is reductive. (1) Personalisation through short sentences. (2) The passive, downcast image. (3) Hyperbole and guilt-inducing imperative. Evaluation: effective fundraising, but it risks stereotyping and a saviour narrative.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "Discuss how two works you have studied use setting to explore the operation of power."

Write a comparative thesis statement and a three-point outline for an essay that answers this question with reference to two literary works you have studied.
items.answer: Model thesis: Achebe and Atwood both make setting an instrument of power, but Achebe shows communal spaces of Umuofia being displaced by colonial church and court, whereas Atwood confines Offred within domestic and institutional spaces that make surveillance intimate. Outline: (1) communal versus controlled space: the village gatherings and the egwugwu ceremony versus the Commander's household and the Wall; (2) the arrival of new institutions (church, courthouse) versus Gilead's rebranding of familiar places; (3) narrative perspective: Achebe's third-person communal view versus Offred's restricted first person.
items.markingKey: Model thesis: Achebe and Atwood both make setting an instrument of power, but Achebe shows communal spaces of Umuofia being displaced by colonial church and court, whereas Atwood confines Offred within domestic and institutional spaces that make surveillance intimate. Any suitable works may be credited.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "In what ways do two works you have studied explore the relationship between memory and truth?"

With reference to two works you have studied, write two comparative body paragraphs that analyse how each writer's choices shape meaning and evaluate their effects.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Kazuo Ishiguro's The Remains of the Day and Art Spiegelman's Maus – both are built from retrospective accounts whose reliability matters.) Thesis: Both works expose the gaps between remembered and actual truth, but Ishiguro uses Stevens's self-deceiving narration to make the reader detect what he suppresses, whereas Spiegelman frames Vladek's testimony with Art's present-day questioning so that the making of memory becomes the subject. Points: unreliable narration and omission (Stevens on Lord Darlington and Miss Kenton) versus framed testimony; form: understated formal prose versus the graphic medium and the animal metaphor; what the works suggest about the cost of remembering or refusing to remember. Evaluate whether either work offers access to truth or only to versions of it.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "Discuss the ways in which two works you have studied present conflict between generations."

Write the comparative analysis section of your essay: develop two integrated comparative points, each analysing specific authorial choices in both works.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Arthur Miller's Death of a Salesman and Chinua Achebe's Things Fall Apart – fathers whose ideas of success and masculinity alienate their sons.) Thesis: Both works present fathers whose rigid ideals drive their sons away, but Miller stages Willy and Biff's conflict through memory sequences that blur past and present, while Achebe shows Okonkwo's fear of weakness pushing Nwoye towards the missionaries, linking a family rupture to a cultural one. Points: the father's ideal: being "well liked" versus fear of resembling Unoka; staging and structure: expressionistic flashbacks versus chronological tragedy; the son's rejection: Biff's confrontation versus Nwoye's conversion. Evaluate how far each work blames the father or the society that shaped him.

Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following opinion column on art and artificial intelligence.

Last week a machine won a regional art prize. The judges, to their credit, were embarrassed. The machine, to its credit, was not – it cannot be embarrassed, which is precisely the point. Art has never been about the finished picture alone; it is about a person risking something in public. An algorithm risks nothing. It cannot fail, so it cannot really succeed.

Guiding question: How does the writer use humour and argument to question whether AI can make art?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the writer uses irony to make a philosophical argument feel like common sense. (1) Parallel "to their credit" humour separates human and machine. (2) A redefinition of art as risk. (3) The short declarative and closing paradox. Evaluation: the definition is contestable – humans who use AI may still take risks.

Paper 2 question: "Compare how two works you have studied present a journey, whether literal or metaphorical."

Write a comparative thesis statement and a three-point outline for an essay that answers this question with reference to two literary works you have studied.
items.answer: Model thesis: Both works use a journey into darkness to test civilisation, but Conrad's frame narrative makes Marlow's voyage up the river an ambiguous moral education, whereas McCarthy's father and son move south through a ruined world where carrying "the fire" means preserving goodness. Outline: (1) frame narrative versus spare third-person narration; (2) landscape as moral symbol; (3) endings: the lie to the Intended versus the boy's survival with a new family.

Paper 2 question: "Discuss how two works you have studied present the tension between public and private selves."

Write a comparative thesis statement and a three-point outline for an essay that answers this question with reference to two literary works you have studied.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "In what ways and to what effect do two works you have studied present the tension between individual desire and social expectation?"

With reference to two works you have studied, write two comparative body paragraphs that analyse how each writer's choices shape meaning and evaluate their effects.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Henrik Ibsen's A Doll's House (studied in translation) and F. Scott Fitzgerald's The Great Gatsby – both centre a character whose desires collide with the codes of a class-conscious society, but one is drama and the other first-person retrospective narration, which allows a contrast of form.) Thesis: Both works dramatise desire constrained by social codes, but where Ibsen moves Nora towards a self-assertive break that the audience witnesses directly, Fitzgerald filters Gatsby's desire through Nick's retrospective narration so that it becomes a doomed, elegiac illusion. Points: symbols of desire and constraint: Nora's forbidden macaroons and the stripped Christmas tree versus Gatsby's green light; form: stage directions and the audience's direct view of Nora versus Nick's mediating, partly admiring narration; endings: the slammed door as liberation versus "boats against the current" as defeat. A strong answer evaluates how genre shapes the reader's judgement: the play invites the audience to judge society, the novel to mourn the dreamer.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied use a narrator's voice to shape the reader's sympathies?"

Write the comparative analysis section of your essay: develop two integrated comparative points, each analysing specific authorial choices in both works.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Charlotte Brontë's Jane Eyre and Margaret Atwood's The Handmaid's Tale – first-person female narrators who address the reader.) Thesis: Both narrators win the reader's sympathy by addressing us directly, but Jane's confident retrospective voice ("Reader, I married him") claims control of her story, whereas Offred's fragmented, self-questioning testimony – later framed by the "Historical Notes" – makes sympathy uneasy. Points: direct address and retrospection; reliability and self-correction; framing devices that judge the narrator. Evaluate how the framing changes our trust in each narrator.

Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following advertisement for a language-learning app, published in an in-flight magazine.

[Image: a grandmother and a teenage boy laugh across a kitchen table in Lisbon; steam rises from two cups.]
She never learned English. He never learned Portuguese. Until now.
Fifteen minutes a day. That's all it takes to turn 'Olá' into a conversation.
Lingo Bridge – because some words can't wait for a translator.
Download free. First month on us.

Guiding question: How does the advertisement use the representation of family to sell a product?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the advertisement sells an app by selling reconnection across generations. (1) The image of facing figures in a warm kitchen enacts the brand metaphor of a bridge. (2) Parallel sentences and the fragment "Until now" create a mini-narrative with the app as the turning point. (3) The low-commitment offer removes barriers. Evaluation: the text idealises language learning, implying fluency is quick, and turns family intimacy into a commercial promise.

Read the following opinion column published in a national newspaper.

Let me be clear: I am no technophobe. I file this column from a laptop, on a train, while my phone buzzes like a trapped wasp. But I have watched my own students in Nairobi sit side by side at lunch, heads bowed, in total silence, as if at a funeral. We would never let a casino open in a school corridor. Why, then, do we allow a slot machine in every pocket?

Guiding question: How does the writer persuade readers that smartphones are harmful to students?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the writer persuades through credibility and analogy rather than data. (1) The concession establishes balance. (2) Similes (wasp, funeral) give emotional, sensory weight. (3) The casino analogy and rhetorical question reframe phones as addictive. Evaluation: the argument relies on anecdote and a loaded analogy; a reader may want evidence.

Paper 2 question: "How do two works you have studied explore the consequences of a single decision?"

Write the comparative analysis section of your essay: develop two integrated comparative points, each analysing specific authorial choices in both works.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Shakespeare's Othello and Ian McEwan's Atonement – a jealous murder and a false accusation.) Points: the moment of decision; dramatic irony versus metafictional revelation; responsibility and guilt. Evaluate which work makes the reader complicit.

Read the following extract from a youth climate movement's manifesto.

WE ARE NOT ASKING.
1. We demand that our city ends approval of new fossil-fuel projects by 2030.
2. We demand climate education in every school, in every subject.
3. We demand a seat at every table where our future is decided.
We are told to be patient. Patience is a luxury for those who will not live with the consequences. Join us.

Guiding question: How does the manifesto construct a powerful collective voice?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the manifesto replaces requests with demands. (1) Capitalised opening. (2) Numbered anaphoric demands. (3) Aphorism and imperative. Evaluation: forceful and clear, though its uncompromising tone may alienate moderates.

Read the following opinion column in an English-language newspaper in Lisbon.

My grandmother's street in Alfama now has eleven bakeries and no neighbours. The bakeries sell pastéis de nata to people who will leave on Sunday; the neighbours who once bought bread there have left for good, priced out by short-term rentals. Tourism, we are told, is our salvation. Perhaps. But a city that sells its every doorway eventually has nothing left to show its visitors except itself, emptied.

Guiding question: How does the writer convey the effects of tourism on a local community?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the writer uses irony and contrast to show that tourism empties what it sells. (1) The juxtaposition of bakeries and neighbours. (2) The ironic "we are told" and minor sentence "Perhaps." undermine the official story. (3) The doorway metaphor and final "emptied" present the city as stripped of life. Evaluation: persuasive through personal voice, though it gives no data on housing.

items.stem:
Paper 2 question: "Compare the ways in which two works you have studied present a character's struggle with identity."

With reference to two works you have studied, write two comparative body paragraphs that analyse how each writer's choices shape meaning and evaluate their effects.
items.answer: Indicative content (example pairing: Marjane Satrapi's Persepolis and Jhumpa Lahiri's The Namesake – both explore identity across cultures, through a graphic memoir and a third-person novel.) Paper 1 – Guided textual analysis (SL: 1 hour 15 minutes for one text; HL: 2 hours 15 minutes for two texts).

Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

Guiding question: How does the speaker turn the accusation of being "unreasonable" against her opponents?

Write a guided textual analysis of the text. You may respond to the guiding question or develop your own focus on how the text creates meaning.
items.answer: Thesis: the speaker reclaims "reasonable" to argue that the law, not the women, is irrational. (1) The ironic "Very well" accepts the label only to test it. (2) Anaphoric rhetorical questions and the personal example of the mother build a logical case. (3) The antithesis citizen/child exposes legal contradiction; the final vow justifies escalation. Evaluation: addressing the press directly anticipates hostile reporting and frames the meeting's message for a wider public.
